title: The first khatm
hook: the last page, a finger under the line, a family pretending not to listen

segments.voice: Yesterday, teaching prayer, and your line: teach by praying. Did someone younger see you do something good? Today, the day a child reaches the last page. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-five.

A child sits cross-legged with a big book on a little wooden stand, a finger moving under the lines, voice careful. The teacher leans in. The family is in the doorway, pretending not to listen. It's the last page. A few short surahs left, then the final line of al-Nas, and it's done: the whole Qur'an, read through, out loud, from the opening to the end. In some homes and mosques, that moment gets a party: new clothes, sweets, guests, the child reading the closing surahs in front of everyone. Today's word is that finish.
screen: `A FINGER UNDER THE LINE.` → `THE LAST PAGE.` → `THE WHOLE BOOK, READ THROUGH.`

segments.voice: Khatm means a completion: a full reading of the Qur'an, from the opening to the end. Adults do it too, alone or together, sometimes over a single month. But a child's first khatm can take years of small daily lessons to reach. Why celebrate it? Start with a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase: the best of you are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it. The child has learned. And someone, a parent, a teacher, an imam, has taught. A khatm party honors both halves of that sentence at once. Second, the struggle counts. In another hadith, in Bukhari and Muslim, in paraphrase: the one who is skilled at reciting the Qur'an is with the noble, righteous scribes, and the one who recites it haltingly, finding it hard, has a double reward. Hear that from the child's side. Every stumble over a long word along the way wasn't wasted. In this hadith, the struggling reader is the one promised two rewards. Third, the book says it can be carried. In surah al-Qamar, in Pickthall's translation: "And in truth We have made the Qur'an easy to remember." A child at a little stand, closing the last page, is that verse in a living room. Fourth, it doesn't really end. Some families mark the khatm by having the child turn straight back to the beginning and read al-Fatiha again, right there. Finish, and start again. The celebration isn't for being done. It's for being on the way.
screen: `LEARN IT AND TEACH IT.` · `THE HALTING READER: A DOUBLE REWARD.` · `EASY TO REMEMBER.` · `FINISH, AND START AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The practice: celebrate a child's learning. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a child who has finished something lately: a book, a school year, a song on an instrument, the alphabet. Or remember your own first finish, and who was there for it. Think of one small way to mark it today: a message, a treat, simply saying, I saw how hard you worked. If you pray, you can thank Allah for their learning in your own words. If you don't, just let yourself be glad for them, slowly. The bell holds the time.
The first khatm. A child's first complete reading of the Qur'an, and the celebration some families give it. Today's word.
Your line: a child finishes. Today, tell one young learner you noticed how hard they worked, not just how well they did. Tomorrow, coming of age. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: In some Muslim communities, a child who finishes reading the whole Qur'an for the first time is honored with a gathering, where the child recites the closing surahs and the family thanks the teacher; the customs and names vary by culture.
